rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the full elution window without excessive compression. This should reveal whether retention is concentrated in a narrow phi range and whether any compounds are still only eluting during the high-organic hold.

All peaks eluted well within the gradient, so trim the phi window to the apparent elution region to improve time efficiency while keeping similar selectivity. This should test whether the cluster around rows 5–7 can be spread without losing any compounds or forcing late hold elution.

The narrow low-phi window over-retained the last compound, so return to the broad window and now halve tG to probe slope sensitivity while improving run time. This will show whether the critical mid-cluster pair compresses strongly with a steeper gradient or is largely slope-insensitive and better attacked with temperature next.

The steeper gradient greatly improved time but collapsed the critical 5–7 cluster, so move to an intermediate slope between 10 and 20 min. This should recover resolution for the slope-sensitive pair while keeping the run substantially shorter than the 20 min method.

The worst pair is clearly slope-sensitive, and moving from 10 to 14 min nearly fixed it without incurring a time penalty, so test a slightly shallower gradient. This may push the 6/7 pair above the resolution threshold while likely keeping the run-time term at zero.

At 16 min all pairs are resolved but the time penalty begins, so the best path is likely to keep the faster 14 min slope and use temperature to improve the remaining 6/7 selectivity. A modest drop in T may separate that close pair while still keeping the run-time term at zero.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so test the opposite direction at the fast 14 min gradient. This will show whether the critical cluster improves with higher temperature and may beat the current best if 6/7 separates without introducing a new overlap.

Temperature moves made the critical cluster worse, so the robust optimum likely lies in slope, between 16 and 20 min. Test 18 min to see whether it maintains full resolution like 16 min but with a smaller time penalty, potentially surpassing the current best.

Since slope is near-optimal at 14 min but temperature clearly changes which pair is critical, test a larger downward temperature step to look for a selectivity crossover that could resolve the cluster differently. This is a focused selectivity probe around the current best time-efficient gradient.

Temperature is clearly not helping, so keep the best slope and test a slightly narrower but still broad phi window to alter selectivity modestly without risking hold elution. This may improve the stubborn mid-cluster separation while preserving the zero time penalty.

The narrower broad window improved the critical pair at 14 min, so now test a slightly shallower slope within that better selectivity window. This is the most direct route to push the 6/7 pair above threshold while likely keeping the time penalty at zero or very small.

The slight window trim from 0.05–0.95 to 0.10–0.90 improved selectivity, so test one more symmetric narrowing at the same optimal 14 min slope. This may further separate the critical mid-cluster while still keeping all peaks inside the gradient and the run-time term at zero.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so this injection is a local robustness check to see whether one more symmetric narrowing preserves the optimum or starts to overcompress the early peaks. If it degrades, injection 12 remains the clear best method.

A second window narrowing also retained the maximum CRF, so continue the local search to find the narrowest broad window that still preserves perfect performance. This tests where early peaks begin to crowd or retention starts to become inefficient.

The failure at 0.25–0.75 shows phi0 is the limiting edge, so probe an asymmetric window that keeps the successful lower bound while trimming only the upper end. This tests whether we can retain perfect performance with a slightly tighter high-organic limit than injection 12.

With CRF already at the maximum, the remaining opportunity is to see whether a slightly steeper gradient can keep full resolution in the better 0.15–0.85 window while shortening the method further. This directly tests whether injection 12 has slope margin or is at the edge of the critical 6/7 separation.

Both 0.15–0.85 and 0.20–0.80 give perfect CRF, while 0.25–0.75 fails from the low end, so test an asymmetric shift that raises only phi0. This will map the boundary of acceptable phi0 and identify whether the optimum plateau extends to a slightly tighter low end without sacrificing resolution.

Raising phi0 hurts before lowering phi1 does, so now probe the opposite asymmetry by keeping the successful phi0=0.15 and extending only the upper end. This checks whether the perfect-CRF plateau includes a slightly wider high-organic limit while preserving all separations.

We already know 0.20–0.80 at 14 min reaches the maximum CRF, so test whether that equally good window tolerates a shorter 12 min gradient. This is a final efficiency probe around a known optimum plateau to see if perfect performance can be maintained at faster slope.

We already have maximum-CRF methods, so use a remaining shot to map temperature robustness of the optimum window more completely. A stronger low-temperature shift may reveal a distinct selectivity regime, but if not, it further confirms 40 C as the best operating point.

The strong low-temperature failure at 0.15–0.85 may partly reflect early-window crowding, so test the other max-CRF window at the same temperature to separate temperature effects from window effects. This will tell us whether the optimum plateau shifts under colder conditions or whether 25 C is broadly unfavorable.

Low temperature is broadly unfavorable, so use a remaining shot to bracket the optimum window on the high-temperature side beyond 45 C. This tests whether there is any narrow selectivity improvement above 40 C, though 40 C currently remains the benchmark.

Complete the high-temperature check on the second max-CRF window to confirm whether 40 C is the unique best temperature across the optimum plateau. This is a final robustness comparison between the two perfect methods under the same hotter condition.

With the maximum already secured, use the penultimate injection to finish bracketing the high-temperature side of the best method. This confirms whether selectivity continues to deteriorate above 50 C or if any unexpected recovery appears.

The final injection should mirror the 55 C test on the second max-CRF window, completing the comparison of the two optimum methods across temperature. This may reveal whether one of the two perfect 40 C methods is more robust at elevated temperature, while injection 12 remains the current best.
